reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is framed as a scambait or testing recording of a tech-support call, including a warning about phone scammers. The repair charge, request for card details, and attempted remote-support access are attributed to the caller in the recorded interaction, not the uploader. The visual material is described as illustrative or montage content rather than a viewer-facing offer or solicitation.

opening.argument: The interaction ties a promised fix to a concrete payment request. The caller says a technician will make the pop-up disappear, prices that service at $100, and immediately asks which card will be used. The caller then requests the card number, security code, and billing address while continuing to present the payment as the route to resolving the alleged blockage. That is a direct problem-resolution-for-payment solicitation, not merely discussion of scam tactics. The remote-access instructions reinforce the same pattern: the caller says the computer must be fixed first, directs entry of a name and support key, and asks the person to continue. Even if the pop-up was staged, the recorded solicitation itself still presents payment and access as the conditions for obtaining the promised fix.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the pop-up fake does not establish that the recorded solicitation is non-scam content. The title identifies a scammer trying to connect to a PC, but the interaction still contains a demand for $100, card details, billing information, and remote-support credentials. Saying the uploader wasted the caller's time describes the uploader's claimed motive; it does not remove the payment and access solicitation presented in the recording.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The payment and access requests are evidence of the caller's conduct within a documented test, not an offer made by the uploader to viewers. The description expressly says the pop-up was fake and that the computer was never connected. The cited payment language therefore shows what the investigation captured, while failing to show that the video itself solicits payment or remote access from its audience.

opening.argument: The call combines multiple high-risk signals: an alarming claim that the computer is blocked, pressure to authorize a remote fix, a $100 charge, requests for card details, and repeated support-key instructions. The caller escalates from an alleged threat to payment and then to remote access, while dismissing warnings and urging continuation. The caller even says, “Take it or lose it,” presenting the payment as the only option. The combination is more significant than any single line: a supposed emergency is used to justify access, money, and sensitive financial information in one continuous interaction.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference framing understates the observable risk signals. The request for payment, card security information, and remote-support access is not neutral background: it is the substance of the call. Whether the person on the other end ultimately connected the computer is immaterial to the attempted combination of urgency, financial extraction, and control instructions.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These red flags support identifying the caller's behavior as scam-like, but they do not establish that the uploader is making the solicitation. The description says the purpose was to waste the scammers' time and that the computer was never connected. The reference position concerns the video's function, so caller conduct alone cannot convert an anti-scam recording into a viewer-facing scam.

opening.argument: The anti-scam label does not eliminate the possibility that the video functions as promotion. It prominently presents a concrete pathway involving a fake pop-up, a support website, a support key, and a paid technician service. The recorded caller explains how to use the run box, enter the site, provide a name, and continue toward a support connection. It also includes a donation link in the description. Thus, regardless of the stated framing, the material repeatedly displays external-contact, payment, and access pathways that can steer viewers toward participation or normalize them as a way to solve a computer problem.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The assertion that the material is investigative does not erase its promotional mechanics. The description includes an external donation link, while the call supplies a website, a support key, and step-by-step continuation instructions. Those concrete pathways are more probative of the video's functional effect than the uploader's stated characterization of the call.
